t.2.8.1: But Mantharā, resenting her and casting aside that ornament, then spoke these words, filled with anger and sorrow.
t.2.8.2: Foolish woman, why have you shown this joy so out of place? Do you not see that you yourself stand in the midst of an ocean of sorrow?
t.2.8.3: Fortunate indeed is Kausalyā, whose son will be consecrated tomorrow, under the Puṣya constellation, by the foremost of the twice-born, to the great office of crown prince.
t.2.8.5: Rāma's chief women will surely be delighted, while your daughters-in-law will be joyless at the ruin of Bharata.
t.2.8.4: Like a slave-woman, with hands joined in reverence, you will wait upon Kausalyā, who will have attained the greatest joy, exultant, her enemy struck down.
t.2.8.6: Then, seeing Mantharā speaking and supremely pleased, Queen Kaikeyī praised the virtues of Rāma alone.
t.2.8.8: Long-lived, he will protect his brothers and servants as a father would. Why, O hunchbacked one, are you so distressed on hearing of Rāma's consecration?
t.2.8.7: Rāma knows dharma, has been disciplined by his elders, and is grateful, truthful in speech, and pure. He is the king's eldest son, and therefore he deserves the position of heir apparent.
t.2.8.9: And Bharata too, that bull among men, will surely obtain the kingdom of his fathers and forefathers after Rāma, at the end of a hundred years.
t.2.8.11: Having heard Kaikeyī's words, Mantharā, deeply grieved, heaved a long, hot sigh and said this to Kaikeyī.
t.2.8.10: When such prosperity has come and is now at hand, Mantharā, and there will be good fortune, why are you so tormented? For he serves me even more than he serves Kausalyā.
t.2.8.12: Seeing harm where there is none, out of folly you do not understand yourself, sinking as you are into an ocean of misery made vast by grief and calamity.
t.2.8.13: Rāghava will be king, and so will the son of Rāghava; but Bharata, O Kaikeyī, will be cut off from the royal line.
t.2.8.14: For not all the sons of a king stand in the kingship, O passionate lady; were all of them to be installed, a very great calamity would arise.
t.2.8.15: Therefore, O Kaikeyī, lady of flawless limbs, kings place the reins of the kingdom in the hands of the eldest son, even when the other sons are also virtuous.
t.2.8.16: O affectionate one, that son of yours will be utterly cut off, like one without a protector, both from all comforts and from the royal line.
t.2.8.18: Surely, once Rāma has gained the kingdom free of all rivals, he will have Bharata driven off to another land, or even to the other world.
t.2.8.17: I have come here for your sake, yet you do not understand me, you who wish to give me a reward at the rise of your co-wife.
t.2.8.19: For you had Bharata taken to his maternal uncle's house while he was still a mere boy; and from closeness, affection is born even among things that do not move.
t.2.8.20: For Saumitri will protect Rāma, and Rāghava too will protect Lakṣmaṇa; the brotherly love of those two, like that of the Aśvins, is renowned throughout the worlds.
t.2.8.21: Therefore Rāma will do no harm whatsoever to Lakṣmaṇa; but that Rāma would do harm to Bharata, there is no doubt.
t.2.8.22: Therefore let your son go to the forest straight from the royal palace itself. This indeed pleases me, and it is also greatly to your benefit.
t.2.8.23: Thus there will indeed be good fortune for you and for the party of your kinsmen, if Bharata, in accordance with dharma, obtains his father's kingdom.
t.2.8.24: That son of yours, a mere boy accustomed to comfort, the natural-born rival of Rāma, how will he live, stripped of his fortune, under the power of Rāma, whose fortune has flourished?
t.2.8.25: You ought to protect Bharata, who is being overshadowed by Rāma, like the leader of an elephant herd attacked by a lion in the forest.
t.2.8.26: Rāma's mother, your co-wife, whom you once spurned out of pride because you were the favoured one, how could she not take revenge for that enmity?
t.2.8.27: For when Rāma obtains the earth, Bharata will surely be ruined. Therefore devise this very day the kingdom for your own son and a reason for the banishment of the other.
